name: Sensors Already Make Money
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Quantum Business That's Already Profitable
lesson.summary: While fault-tolerant quantum computing remains a research bet with no proven return, atomic clocks, quantum magnetometers, and quantum gravimeters are sold today under real commercial contracts, generating revenue now rather than as a future promise.
lesson.body:
It is worth pausing on a distinction this book has been building toward: there is a difference between a technology that might someday be worth a great deal of money, and a technology that is worth money today, with invoices being sent and paid. Fault-tolerant quantum computing, the kind capable of running Shor's algorithm on a cryptographically relevant problem or simulating a complex molecule end to end, is still the former. Quantum sensing is the latter, and has been for years.

Atomic clocks are the clearest case, because they are older and more thoroughly embedded in the economy than magnetometers or gravimeters. Every GPS satellite carries atomic clocks, and the entire global positioning system depends on their stability to convert tiny timing differences into position. Financial exchanges use precision timing derived in part from atomic clock references to timestamp trades to the microsecond, a legal requirement in several jurisdictions after high frequency trading disputes made timestamp accuracy a regulatory issue. Telecommunications networks synchronize using atomic clock references to keep cell towers and data centers coordinated. None of this is speculative. It is infrastructure that has been running, and being paid for, for decades.

Magnetometers and gravimeters are newer to market but follow the same pattern rather than a hoped for one. Companies building optically pumped magnetometers sell clinical MEG systems to hospitals and research universities today, with regulatory clearance processes already underway or completed in multiple countries. Mining and oil exploration firms contract survey companies to run quantum gravimeter surveys over prospective sites, paying for the survey the same way they would pay for a seismic survey, because the gravimeter data narrows down drilling targets and reduces the number of expensive exploratory wells needed. Utility companies pay engineering firms that use gravimeters to locate buried infrastructure before construction, because the alternative, cutting into the wrong pipe, is a categorically more expensive mistake.

This matters for how a skeptical reader should weigh quantum computing headlines against quantum sensing headlines. A press release about a new qubit count or a new error correction milestone is a claim about future capability, resting on a chain of assumptions about scaling that have not yet been demonstrated at the necessary scale. A quantum sensing company's revenue is a fact about the present, verifiable the same way any other company's revenue is verifiable, through contracts, shipped units, and financial statements. That does not make quantum sensing companies safe investments in some absolute sense, and later chapters will address the risks that remain, but it does mean the core technology risk, whether the physics itself can be turned into a working, sellable product, has already been retired for sensing in a way it has not for fault-tolerant computing.
